title: Digits moved one pixel
objectives: Test a CNN and a same-size MLP on digits shifted one pixel, and explain the gap.

screens.title: Move it one pixel
screens.prose: Here is a held-out 2 that the CNN of l10 and a same-size MLP (64-40-10, 3,010 parameters, trained the same way) both read correctly. Now move it one pixel right.

state.caption: A held-out 2, and the same 2 moved one pixel right with a zero column filled in on the left.

screens.question: Which net still reads the moved digit as a 2?

options.text: The CNN only
Both nets
options.why: The MLP now reads it as a 3.

options.text: The MLP only
options.why: The CNN still reads 2, with probability 0.69.

options.text: Neither net
options.why: One of them still reads 2.

hints.text: Which net reuses the same weights at every position?
The CNN slides each filter; the MLP has one weight per pixel.
A shift moves the ink onto pixels whose MLP weights never saw this stroke there.

feedback.correct: The CNN reads 2 (probability 0.69); the MLP reads 3 (0.75).
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about how each net looks at pixels.

explain.text: A convolution applies the same filter everywhere, so the shifted strokes still light up the same maps. The MLP’s 2,560 first-layer weights are tied to fixed pixels, and the shifted 2 reads as a 3.

screens.title: Further
screens.prose: Slide the same 2 from two pixels left to two pixels right and watch what each net reads.

state.caption: Shift 0: the CNN reads 2, the MLP reads 2.

frames.caption: Shift -2: the CNN reads 2, the MLP reads 5.
Shift -1: the CNN reads 2, the MLP reads 2.
Shift 0: the CNN reads 2, the MLP reads 2.
Shift +1: the CNN reads 2, the MLP reads 3.
Shift +2: the CNN reads 3, the MLP reads 3.

screens.question: At which shift to the right does the CNN first misread this 2?

hints.text: Move the slider to the right, one step at a time.
At +1 the CNN still reads 2.
At +2 it reads 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Watch the caption as you slide right.

byKey.mlp: That is where the MLP first misreads. The CNN holds on one step further.

explain.text: The CNN survives one pixel and fails at two, reading 3; the MLP fails already at one. On an 8 by 8 image a shift of 2 pixels is a quarter of the width.

screens.title: Why the CNN holds
screens.prose: A convolution is **shift-equivariant** (level 1): shift the input and its feature maps shift with it. Max pooling (level 2) then forgives a little movement inside each 2 by 2 window.
screens.question: Why does the MLP lose the moved 2?

options.text: Its weights are tied to pixels, so moved ink meets other weights
It has fewer parameters than the CNN has
options.why: It has more: 3,010 against 2,730.

options.text: It was trained for fewer epochs than the CNN
options.why: Both were trained the same way, 30 epochs.

options.text: Its hidden layer has no ReLU to bend it
options.why: It has a ReLU hidden layer, as `stat-learning` l17’s net did.

hints.text: Where is each net’s first weight tied?
A conv filter is the same at all 64 positions.
The MLP’s 64 inputs each have their own 40 weights.

feedback.correct: Tied to pixels: moved ink meets weights trained for other strokes.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare how each first layer is tied to positions.

explain.text: The MLP learned "ink at pixel 37 means 2" pixel by pixel. The CNN’s filters learned strokes wherever they sit, and pooling absorbs part of the move.

screens.title: All 540, on three seeds
screens.prose: Shift every held-out digit by 0, 1 or 2 pixels in each of four directions and average. Each model was trained on three seeds.

state.caption: Mean over the four directions (right, left, down, up), zero fill. One bar per seed.

screens.question: For the supplied CNN, what is the mean accuracy over the four one-pixel shifts? Give a decimal to 2 places.

hints.text: Read the 1 px group.
The CNN bars of seed 0.
The four shifts give 0.657, 0.663, 0.494, 0.657.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the CNN’s four one-pixel accuracies.

byKey.mlp: That is the MLP. The CNN’s bars are higher.
byKey.clean: That is the CNN on unshifted digits.

explain.text: One pixel costs the CNN over a third of its accuracy (0.99 to 0.62) and the MLP more than half (0.97 to 0.45). At two pixels both fall below 0.2.

screens.title: Why the CNN still drops
screens.prose: Equivariance holds up to the pool. After it, the dense layer has its own 10 weights for each of the 256 pooled values, just as the MLP has its own 40 for each pixel.

state.caption: l6’s map: a shift of one column moves values across the 2 by 2 windows.

screens.question: Which part of the CNN is not shift-tolerant?

options.text: The dense layer after pooling, tied to positions
The convolution of the first layer
options.why: It is equivariant: its maps move with the input.

options.text: The ReLU after the convolution
options.why: It acts on each value alone and does not care where the value is.

options.text: The softmax at the very end
options.why: It acts on the ten scores, after positions are gone.

hints.text: Which layer has a weight per position?
The dense layer reads 256 pooled values in a fixed order.
A shift moves values across pool windows (l6), into other dense weights.

feedback.correct: The dense layer: one weight for every pooled position.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the layer with a weight per position.

explain.text: A one-pixel shift moves some values into the next pool window, so the pooled map changes, and the dense layer reads every position with its own weight. Tolerance ends there.

screens.title: Teach both to shift
screens.prose: An honest comparison gives the MLP the same help. Train both again on the 1,005 training digits plus four copies shifted one pixel: 5,025 images, 10 epochs.
screens.question: On three seeds the augmented CNN scores above 0.96 on one-pixel shifts. About how large is the gap between the augmented CNN and the augmented MLP?

options.text: Under 0.05
Between 0.05 and 0.10
options.why: The augmented MLP lands above 0.93 on every seed.

options.text: About 0.17, as before
options.why: Augmenting closes most of the gap: the MLP has now seen shifted digits.

options.text: Over 0.20
options.why: The gap shrinks with augmentation, not grows.

hints.text: Read the MLP row with shifted copies.
It reaches 0.951.
Compare with 0.96.

feedback.correct: Under 0.05: on the three seeds the gaps are 0.019, 0.023, 0.022.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the augmented MLP with the augmented CNN.

explain.text: Shifted copies teach the MLP these four shifts: its shifted accuracy rises from 0.45 to 0.95. The gap falls under 0.05, against 0.17 before. At two pixels, which the copies never showed, the gap returns to between 0.06 and 0.10 on the validation digits.

screens.title: Shift-invariant?
screens.prose: A report says: "CNNs are shift-invariant, so moving a digit cannot change the answer." Our CNN falls from 0.99 to 0.62 on one-pixel shifts.
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: It is partly tolerant, not invariant
It is shift-invariant; the drop is a bug
options.why: The drop is what the design predicts: only the convolution moves with the input.

options.text: It has no shift tolerance at all
options.why: They do have some: 0.62 against the MLP’s 0.45.

options.text: Pooling makes any shift harmless
options.why: A 2 by 2 pool absorbs at most part of a one-pixel move, and nothing of two pixels.

hints.text: Which layers move with the input?
Convolution: yes. Pooling: a little. Dense: no.
So the net is tolerant, not invariant.

feedback.correct: Partly tolerant, by design and by pooling.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each layer for what a shift does to it.

byKey.b: You took "shift-invariant" literally. The drop to the one-pixel score is the measured tolerance, not a bug.

explain.text: Equivariance plus a little pooling is tolerance, not invariance: the drop from 0.99 to 0.62 measures it. A global pool or augmentation would add more.

screens.title: Ink off the edge
screens.prose: This held-out 7 has ink in its last column. Moved one pixel right, that column falls off the 8 by 8 image, and a zero column comes in on the left.
screens.question: How many inked pixels are lost?

hints.text: Look at the last column only.
Count the cells that are not 0.
Grey levels 10, 6, 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the non-zero cells of the last column.

byKey.column: That is the whole column. Only the inked cells carry information.
byKey.none: Zero fill adds blanks on the left; the inked cells on the right are lost.

explain.text: Zero fill keeps the image 8 by 8, so 3 inked pixels of the top stroke vanish. Some shifts change a digit itself, not just its place.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from cnn_ops_l3 import load_split, load_weights, predict, cnn_logits, mlp_logits, shift_images

X_tr, y_tr, X_va, y_va, X_te, y_te = load_split()
cnn = load_weights('cnn-w-exit.json')
mlp = load_weights('cnn-w-mlp.json')
cnn_predict = lambda X: predict(cnn_logits, cnn, X)
mlp_predict = lambda X: predict(mlp_logits, mlp, X)
SHIFTS = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]   # right, left, down, up


def shifted_accuracy(predict_fn, X, y, shifts):
    return [float((predict_fn(shift_images(X, dx, dy)) == y).mean()) for dx, dy in shifts]


def margin(cnn_acc, mlp_acc):
    return cnn_acc - mlp_acc >= 0.10 - 1e-9

tests.call: margin(float(np.mean(shifted_accuracy(cnn_predict, X_te, y_te, SHIFTS))), float(np.mean(shifted_accuracy(mlp_predict, X_te, y_te, SHIFTS))))

tests.setup: mlp_aug = load_weights('cnn-w-mlp-aug.json'); aug_predict = lambda X: predict(mlp_logits, mlp_aug, X)
tests.call: margin(float(np.mean(shifted_accuracy(cnn_predict, X_te, y_te, SHIFTS))), float(np.mean(shifted_accuracy(aug_predict, X_te, y_te, SHIFTS))))

widget.how: Submit runs 7 hidden tests on the supplied weights. Three check accuracies to $10^{-9}$: the four one-pixel shifts for the CNN and for the MLP, then a no-shift and a two-pixel case. Four check the margin: against the MLP (met), against an MLP trained on shifted copies (not met), two planted pairs, and a pair whose gap is exactly 0.10 on paper. The 540 images take about a second in all.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: Mean accuracy over the four one-pixel shifts, zero fill: $$\bar a = \tfrac{1}{4}\sum_{(dx, dy)} a(dx, dy), \qquad \text{margin met when } \bar a_{\text{CNN}} - \bar a_{\text{MLP}} \ge 0.10.$$ The number script set 0.10 on the shifted validation digits, not the test digits: there the CNN led the MLP by at least 0.17 on every pair of three seeds, and by under 0.03 once the MLP trained on shifted copies.

screens.title: One day late
screens.prose: A model reads a grid of 20 days by 8 features for each stock. Trained on one market, it is run on another whose data feed stamps every feature one day late.
screens.question: What is the honest way to judge the model before trusting it on the live market?

options.text: Test it on data shifted one day, or held out from the live market
Report its accuracy on the training market’s test split
options.why: That split has no lag, so it overstates live accuracy.

options.text: Assume a convolution over days makes it immune to lags
options.why: Tolerance is partial, as the digits showed; it has to be measured.

options.text: Retrain until training accuracy is higher
options.why: A higher training score says nothing about the lagged market.

hints.text: What did the digits teach about a shift?
The clean score of 0.99 fell to 0.62 on one-pixel shifts.
Test on the shift you expect.

feedback.correct: Test on the shift you expect: the honest test is out of distribution.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The live data are shifted; the test should be too.

explain.text: A one-day lag is a shift along the time axis. Built-in tolerance helps, augmenting with lagged copies helps more, and only a shifted test says how much.

ideas: Convolution is shift-equivariant and pooling forgives a little, so a CNN degrades less than an MLP, which has a weight for every pixel.
On the four one-pixel shifts the supplied CNN keeps 0.62 and the MLP 0.45: a gap above the rule of 0.10 on all three seeds. At two pixels both fall below 0.2.
Training on shifted copies lifts the MLP above 0.93 and shrinks the gap below 0.05: compare models with the same data.

formula.note: Mean accuracy over the four one-pixel shifts, zero fill.

Nothing changes compared with zero fill
options.why: Zero fill leaves the first column empty; roll fills it with the last column.

options.text: It moves the digit down instead of right
options.why: With the right axis, roll moves it right too.

options.text: It blurs the digit across neighbours
options.why: Roll moves pixels without mixing them.

feedback.correct: Roll wraps; zero fill does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Where does the last column go?

explain.text: `np.roll` treats the image as a ring, so ink that leaves on the right comes back on the left.

options.text: Average each map over all positions before the dense layer
Add a second dense layer after the first
options.why: A dense layer is tied to positions; another one adds no tolerance.

options.text: Remove the max pool between the layers
options.why: Pooling is part of the tolerance; removing it loses some.

options.text: Use a larger learning rate for training
options.why: The rate changes how training goes, not what the layers can represent.

feedback.correct: A global average pool removes position before the dense layer.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which layer is tied to positions?

explain.text: Averaging each map over all positions leaves 16 numbers that ignore where a feature sat, so a small shift barely changes them.
